title: Cellar and Harvest
premise: Urban explorer Odile Galloway descends beneath the dying village of Hollowmere to map tunnels absent from every survey, documenting each step as an act of devotion. When the church bell—melted down in 1911—rings at midnight, the tunnels seal behind them and Odile is trapped with the village's last six residents, who know exactly what the ringing summons. To survive until sunrise, Odile must uncover the century-old pact the founders made with something in the dry well, and choose between sealing it forever and sparing Tam, the bell-keeper's grandson who has already been half-invited in. The story ends with dawn: Odile breaks the pact by giving the thing what it actually wanted—an honest witness—and the village burns its records, freeing Tam, though Odile carries the tunnels in their dreams ever after.
about_author: Yara Whitlock is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing parish records from abandoned English villages before turning to horror. They write about places that remember more than the people who left them.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile arrives in Hollowmere with LiDAR scans showing a tunnel network under the village that appears on no map, county record, or memory. They check into the only inn and begin interviewing locals, who deflect with practiced warmth. Beat: the thrill of discovery curdling into the sense of being expected.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile catalogs the village: the dry well, the roofless church, a boy named Tam who watches them photograph everything. Tam asks, oddly, whether Odile writes down what people tell them. Beat: loneliness meeting a first flicker of connection, shadowed by Tam's strange intensity.

chapters.title: Six Names on the Register
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. In the parish archive Odile finds a burial register that stops mid-page in 1911, six names circled, and a ledger of 'offerings' paid to something called the Keeper of the Dry Place. Beat: the investigator's satisfaction turning to dread as the pattern refuses to be mundane.

chapters.title: The Bell That Was Melted
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam tends the empty bell tower at night, a duty his grandmother drilled into him. He hears the rope creak and knows the bell is coming back. He decides not to warn the stranger with the camera. Beat: love of family warring with the knowledge of what duty costs.

chapters.title: Midnight, and It Rings
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The bell rings—a bronze voice from a tower holding no bell—and every door in Hollowmere unlocks at once. The tunnels' entrance behind the well grinds open. Odile, filming, is pulled down with the villagers. Beat: terror and awe fused; the world's rules visibly break.

chapters.title: The Ones Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, with ensemble voices. Trapped below, Odile meets the six remaining villagers: grandmother Maren, twins Ada and Silas, the innkeeper Cobb, deaf weaver Ivetta, and Tam. They explain the rules of the night without explaining the reason. Beat: strangers forced into a found family by circumstance.

chapters.title: Rules for the Dry Place
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren teaches the survival rules: answer nothing in your own voice, don't drink from any water, and when the bell counts, count with it. Odile's instinct to document nearly breaks the first rule within the hour. Beat: competence humbled; the group's fragile trust forming.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Bought
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada shows Odile the original pact: in 1911 the village sold its dead to the Keeper in exchange for the well never refilling and the plague passing them by. The bell was melted to end the payments. It didn't end the debt. Beat: the horror of inherited sin and the hunger for someone to blame.

chapters.title: The First Count
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The bell rings eleven times. Each toll takes something—a memory from Cobb, the twins' shared language, the color from Ivetta's eyes. Odile records it all, and the recording comes back wrong: their own voice answering in a language they don't know. Beat: the cost becomes personal.

chapters.title: Tam's Half-Invitation
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam confesses to Odile that his grandmother began teaching him the Keeper's names, that part of him already answers when called. He asks Odile to write down the truth of him before he's gone—documentation as a kind of prayer, his words now. Beat: love kindling in the worst possible place.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Water rises in the dry well below, black and warm, and with it the Keeper's presence—patient, enormous, almost gentle. Silas, who wanted to leave Hollowmere his whole life, realizes he's the only one who could swim it and live, and that living isn't guaranteed to be his afterward. Beat: despair with a blade of defiance in it.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada proposes killing Tam before the final toll—the pact names a bell-keeper's blood as the closing payment. The group splits. Maren refuses to sacrifice another child to her ancestors' bargain; Cobb argues the village's survival outweighs one life. Beat: the found family fractures over what justice means when no court will ever hear it.

chapters.title: Ivetta's Hands
chapters.summary: Ivetta's POV. Deaf to the bell, Ivetta alone can stand beside the tower and read what it does: the ringing isn't a summons but a question, asked every night for a hundred years, and no one has ever answered it honestly. She signs this to Odile. Beat: revelation—the horror reframed as an unanswered plea.

chapters.title: The Tenth Toll
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Two tolls remain. Cobb, desperate, tries to give the Keeper Odile instead, arguing a stranger owes the village nothing and owes it everything. Tam stops him, and the act costs Tam most of what's left of himself. Beat: betrayal, sacrifice, and Odile's realization that they are no longer an outsider.

chapters.title: What the Keeper Wanted
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren finally reads her grandmother's confession: the 1911 pact was a lie told to the village. The Keeper never wanted blood or payment—only a witness, someone to record what the village did to its own dead, and every generation fled the asking. Beat: grief and terrible clarity; the debt was always truth.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Toll
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The penultimate toll strips the tunnel of light and sound except Odile's notebook and pen. The Keeper comes as the shape of everyone the village buried. Odile, terrified, keeps writing—recording the pact, the murders, the lies—as the only honest act left. Beat: the climax of nerve; documentation as defiance.

chapters.title: An Honest Witness
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile answers the bell's question aloud, in their own voice, with the whole truth of Hollowmere—nothing softened. The Keeper receives the record the way a starving thing receives bread. The twelfth toll never falls. Beat: catharsis; the monster was a wound, and naming it closes it.

chapters.title: Sunrise Terms
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. The half-invitation releases Tam, but the Keeper offers him a choice: stay as its bell-keeper in a quiet world, or walk out human and let the well refill slowly over a hundred years. Tam chooses the sunrise, and Odile. Beat: love against duty, duty losing at last.

chapters.title: The Burning of the Records
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The survivors burn the pact ledger, the offering books, and the register in the roofless church—justice administered by their own hands, since no law ever acknowledged the crime. Maren scatters the ashes into the refilling well. Beat: mourning and release; the past finally allowed to stay past.

chapters.title: Six Become Three
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The costs are counted: Cobb and Silas did not survive the night, and Ivetta chooses to remain near the well as its quiet warden. Odile photographs the survivors—Maren, Ada, Tam—and writes their names into the record properly, fully, as people and not evidence. Beat: grief braided with gratitude; found family made formal.

chapters.title: The Map With a Hole In It
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Weeks later, Odile files their survey with one deliberate omission: the tunnels, now collapsed, marked only as 'unverified.' Some places shouldn't be found. Tam reads the report over their shoulder and laughs for the first time since the bell. Beat: quiet healing; the choice of what not to know.

chapters.title: What Odile Carries
chapters.summary: Tam and Odile's shared POV, alternating. On the road out of Hollowmere, Odile dreams the tunnels each night and writes them down each morning, and Tam keeps watch until the dreams end—or doesn't mind if they don't. The last entry in the notebook is both their names. Beat: resolution—haunted but together, the witness and the kept, walking toward ordinary light.
